analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to buy one million Bitcoins over five years and hold them for twenty years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with zero cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2024 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would direct the Treasury Department to buy up to 200,000 Bitcoins a year for five years — one million in total — and hold them in a government 'Strategic Bitcoin Reserve' for at least 20 years, selling none except to pay down federal debt. All Bitcoin seized by federal agencies would be moved into the reserve instead of auctioned, and states could store their own Bitcoin there. The purchases would be paid for with Federal Reserve earnings that otherwise flow to the Treasury's general fund, plus a smaller Federal Reserve surplus cushion.
analysis.who_benefits: People and companies who already hold large amounts of Bitcoin. A government program buying a million Bitcoins — worth roughly $60 billion at 2024 prices — would create a huge, price-supporting buyer and would make holding Bitcoin look officially sanctioned. The crypto industry gains legitimacy and a permanent federal customer for custody and security services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Existing Bitcoin holders and crypto firms

how_it_helps.text: The Treasury would buy up to 200,000 Bitcoins per year for five years, one million total, and hold them at least 20 years, selling none except to retire federal debt.
A standing government buyer of that size would put sustained upward pressure on Bitcoin's price, directly increasing the value of coins already held by investors and companies.
Bitcoin seized by any federal agency, including the Marshals Service, would be transferred to the reserve rather than sold, removing government sales from the market.
States could store their Bitcoin in segregated accounts inside the federal reserve, deepening the government's entanglement with the asset.
The bill affirms that individuals keep full rights to hold and self-custody their own Bitcoin.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the general public. The purchases would be funded by the first $6 billion of Federal Reserve net earnings remitted to Treasury each year from 2025 through 2029 — money that otherwise reduces the deficit — and the Fed's required surplus cushion would be cut from $6.825 billion to $2.4 billion. If Bitcoin's price falls over the 20-year hold, the public absorbs the loss; the program's upside is speculative and wouldn't be realized for decades.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, via diverted Federal Reserve earnings

drawbacks.text: The government would commit tens of billions of dollars to a single, historically volatile asset whose price has repeatedly fallen more than 70% from peaks, with no way to sell for 20 years except to retire debt.

The funding mechanism diverts Federal Reserve earnings to the Treasury that would otherwise count against the deficit, and shrinks the Fed's loss-absorbing surplus from $6.825 billion to $2.4 billion, slightly weakening the central bank's finances.

A guaranteed government buyer would directly raise the value of an asset held by a small set of large investors — a transfer of public money toward concentrated wealth with no corresponding public service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for the public is purely speculative: the government's coins might be worth more in 20 years, and they could be used to retire debt. The cost is immediate and certain: $6 billion a year of Federal Reserve earnings redirected, a thinner Fed surplus cushion, and a program engineered to raise the price of an asset whose main beneficiaries are people who already own it. The bill's own findings lean on analogies to gold reserves, but Bitcoin has none of gold's history of stability. On the evidence, the costs are concrete and the benefits are a bet placed with public money.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cynthia Lummis introduced the BITCOIN Act on July 31, 2024; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor; the bill ended with zero cosponsors.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill would have required Treasury to buy one million Bitcoins over five years and hold them at least 20 years, funded by Federal Reserve remittances and a reduced Fed surplus.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers came out ahead: the public avoided a $6 billion-a-year program whose guaranteed effect was to raise the price of an asset held largely by wealthy investors. Crypto holders lost the chance at that price support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who avoided funding the reserve

for.name: Sen. Cynthia Lummis
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wyoming; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it no further than referral; no cosponsor ever joined.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so the partisan shape of the bill is unknown beyond its single Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Bitcoin holders and the cryptocurrency industry
industries.note: The bill would make the federal government a guaranteed large buyer of Bitcoin and lock in official custody of seized coins, putting sustained upward pressure on the price of coins already held by large investors. Its main certain effect is a transfer of public funds toward the value of concentrated crypto holdings.

The bill cuts the Fed's required surplus from $6.825 billion to $2.4 billion and diverts the first $6 billion of annual net earnings remittances to buying Bitcoin, weakening the central bank's financial cushion while funding the program.

Building and auditing a nationwide network of secure Bitcoin storage facilities, with quarterly cryptographic attestations and independent auditors, would create new government contracts for firms with crypto-custody and security expertise.
